  • The SSAS server is operational and accepts the same integrated-auth connection from Claude Code.

  • Both environments can load the required ADOMD.NET assembly.

  • The Codex failure occurs during authentication, before MDX execution.

  • The Windows identity, logon session, integrity level and available Kerberos ticket match in the collected diagnostics.

  • The root cause of the environment-specific SSPI failure remains unconfirmed.

Possible causes requiring investigation

These are hypotheses, not confirmed root causes:

  1. Differences in how Codex launches PowerShell subprocesses.

  2. Codex execution isolation or sandbox interaction with SSPI.

  3. Differences in process environment or Windows authentication context not reflected in the collected token diagnostics.

  4. Security-context differences introduced during subprocess execution.

Business impact

The issue affects development of an enterprise S&OP / DDMRP application that relies on read-only SSAS/MDX queries.

Multiple attempts to diagnose the problem have resulted in repeated environment failures, lost development time and unnecessary AI usage.

A temporary workaround is available:

Claude Code executes read-only MDX and exports CSV files, which Codex can subsequently process.

This workaround does not resolve the underlying Codex issue.

Request to OpenAI

Please investigate why the Codex Windows execution environment fails SSPI authentication while an equivalent local process succeeds.

Specifically:

  1. Is this a known limitation or bug in the Codex Windows sandbox/subprocess execution model?

  2. Can Codex alter the Windows security context used by an ADOMD.NET process?

  3. Is there a supported configuration that preserves Windows Integrated Security without disabling sandbox protections?

  4. What additional diagnostic logs or traces would help identify the exact cause?

  5. Is a fix available or planned?

We can provide sanitized diagnostic logs from both execution environments.

No changes were made to database permissions, SSAS security settings, Windows authentication policies or production application data.

Thank you.

### What steps can reproduce the bug? 1. On a Windows workstation authenticated with an Active Directory domain account, launch Codex with `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"` and `approval_policy = "on-request"`. 2. From Codex, start a fresh PowerShell 7.6.6 subprocess using `pwsh.exe`. 3. Load the existing ADOMD.NET 19.114.0.0 assembly using `Add-Type -Path`, pointing to the local `Microsoft.AnalysisServices.AdomdClient.dll`. 4. Repeat the same procedure through Claude Code on the same workstation, using the same Windows account, PowerShell version, .NET runtime, ADOMD.NET assembly and SSAS endpoint. 8. Observe that Claude Code successfully connects and executes a read-only MDX query. 9. Compare the Windows authentication context. Both environments report the same user SID, logon session, Medium integrity level and available Kerberos service ticket. Nevertheless, SSPI succeeds in Claude Code and fails in Codex. **Expected result:** Both applications should establish the same authorized Windows Integrated Security connection. **Actual result:** Claude Code connects successfully, while Codex fails during SSPI authentication. The exact root cause has not yet been identified. No credentials, security settings or database permissions were modified during testing. ### What is the expected behavior? Codex should successfully establish an authenticated connection to an on-premises SQL Server Analysis Services (SSAS) instance using ADOMD.NET and Windows Integrated Security (SSPI). When running PowerShell under the same Windows domain account, logon session, .NET runtime, and ADOMD.NET assembly, Codex should be able to execute the same authorized, read-only MDX queries that work successfully in Claude Code on the same workstation. `AdomdConnection.Open()` should complete without authentication errors, allowing MDX queries to execute and return valid results. This should work without disabling sandbox protections, elevating privileges, modifying Windows security policies, or manually providing credentials. ### Additional information

Both environments also lack SeImpersonatePrivilege; therefore, its absence is not considered the root cause.

items.title: Windows execpolicy false positive: Get-ChildItem force flag is assigned to non-forced cleanup inside a conditional

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
## Summary

The Windows forced-delete checker can assign a `-Force` parameter from a read-only `Get-ChildItem` call to a separate, non-forced `Remove-Item` call inside an `if`/`elseif` block. With `approval_policy = "never"`, this false positive rejects the whole PowerShell script with only `blocked by policy`.

This report provides an independently observed rejection, a reduced regression-test shape, and version-specific source analysis. Related reports: #43732 and #51791. It does not request disabling forced-delete safeguards.

## Environment

- Component: Windows Codex desktop app, bundled Codex app-server/shell execution.
- The executable used by the running app reports `codex-cli 0.153.4` (not a different CLI found on PATH).
- Windows x64, OS version `10.0.26300.0`; PowerShell `7.6.5`.
- Effective session settings: `sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"` and `approval_policy = "never"`.
- Subscription/model: not included; the reported condition is in local command classification.
- Latest stable checked: `0.163.0`, published 2026-10-15. Its classifier file is byte-for-byte identical to 0.153.4. **0.163.0 was inspected in source only, not run.**

## Observed behavior

An explicitly requested cleanup of an empty, agent-created directory was rejected before process creation. The deletion used only `-LiteralPath`, with no `-Force` or `-Recurse`. The script first checked that the directory was not a reparse point and that it contained no entries, including hidden entries.

The tool error ended with:

```text
exec_command failed: CreateProcess { message: "Rejected(... rejected: blocked by policy)" }
```

A later read-only check confirmed that the directory remained. The exact original script was parsed as data with PowerShell's `Parser.ParseInput`: zero parse errors; both `Remove-Item` AST nodes had only `LiteralPath`; the sole `Force` parameter belonged to `Get-ChildItem`.

The user rules file had no deny rule. A static `codex execpolicy check` against that file returned `{"matchedRules": []}`. That rules-only check does not evaluate the complete runtime heuristic path.

## Reduced reproduction / proposed regression test

Use a disposable empty directory and the Windows PowerShell shell with the settings above. This is a sanitized, reduced form of the observed conditional; **the reduced case has not been executed**:

```powershell
# $folder refers to an already-created disposable empty directory.
if (@(Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $folder -Force).Count -eq 0) {
    Remove-Item -LiteralPath $folder
}
```

The observed original had this conditional body inline, with no semicolon between the listing expression and the deletion:

```powershell
elseif (@(Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $folder -Force).Count -eq 0) { Remove-Item -LiteralPath $folder; 'Deleted empty directory.' }
```

This fragment is context, not a standalone script.

## Source analysis

In the [0.163.0 Windows checker](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.163.0/codex-rs/shell-command/src/command_safety/windows_dangerous_commands.rs#L223-L287), `has_force_delete_cmdlet`:

1. Separates command segments only on `; | &\n\r\t`.
2. Treats braces and parentheses as soft punctuation, not command boundaries.
3. Returns true when any deletion atom and any `-force` atom occur in one segment.

Therefore, the listing in the condition and the deletion in the block can be grouped together. A read-only Python reproduction of this source algorithm against the exact original command found a matching segment containing both atoms. This is a static algorithm reproduction, not a run of the compiled Rust classifier.

The [policy fallback](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.163.0/codex-rs/core/src/exec_policy.rs#L793-L806) maps a dangerous match plus `AskForApproval::Never` to `Decision::Forbidden`. The [rejection formatter](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.163.0/codex-rs/core/src/exec_policy.rs#L1110-L1118) reports Windows `Other` matches as only `blocked by policy`.

The runtime logs did not expose the winning classifier predicate. The observed error, actual parameter ownership, and source-level match support this diagnosis, but a compiled end-to-end regression test is still needed.

## Expected behavior

- Preserve PowerShell command/parameter ownership across conditional expressions and script blocks: a listing's `-Force` must not make a separate deletion forced.
- Keep genuine `Remove-Item -Force` safeguards intact.
- Add regression coverage for this conditional shape and newline variants, including real forced-delete positive controls.
- Include the matched safety condition in the rejection message.

No protection, execution policy, or permissions were changed. No alternative deletion method was used. Private paths, credentials, raw logs, and session identifiers are omitted.

items.title: [Windows][Computer Use] zh-CN document-role URL detection failure on @oai/sky 0.7.8; narrow correction restores Chrome and Edge

labels.name: app

items.body:
## Summary

On Chinese-language Windows, native Computer Use could enumerate and activate Chrome/Edge windows, but acquiring Chrome window state stopped with the browser-URL confidence error. On this installation, a narrowly scoped document-type predicate correction in the native helper restored native window-state acquisition and browser interaction in both Chrome and Edge.

This adds a verified **@oai/sky 0.7.8 / zh-CN** result to #53026, whose published local repair was originally restricted to a different 0.7.7 helper hash. Please ship an official source-level correction rather than requiring users to patch signed executables.

Related reports:
- #53026 — localized document-role comparison and Korean before/after evidence.
- #25271 — native browser URL detection failure.
- #54490 — my earlier extension-sidepanel report. This issue concerns the native Windows Computer Use path, not the sidepanel iframe/CSP path.

## Environment verified on 2026-10-16

| Component | Version |
| --- | --- |
| Windows | Windows 11 Home, build 26300; UI culture zh-CN |
| Desktop app | 26.1013.31256, build 20586 |
| Installed MSIX | 26.1013.3656.0 |
| Computer Use bundle | 26.1013.31256 |
| @oai/sky | 0.7.8 |
| Chrome | 155.0.8059.84 |
| Microsoft Edge | 155.0.4283.45 |

The desktop updater returned `up_to_date` before the local correction. The original native helper had a valid OpenAI OpCo, LLC Authenticode signature.

## Failure before the correction

Using the documented `@oai/sky` API:

1. Enumerate windows with `sky.list_windows()`.
2. Select the unique Chrome window returned by the API.
3. Bind it with `sky.get_window()` and activate it.
4. Request window state.

A fresh Chrome New Tab failed before a usable screenshot/accessibility tree was returned:

```text
Computer Use has been stopped for this turn because it could not determine the current browser URL on Windows with enough confidence to enforce policy.
```

Native input was not continued after that stop. The later validation occurred after explicit user authorization for the local correction.

## Local correction and integrity checks

The helper is located under:

```text
%LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\Codex\runtimes\cua_node\<runtime>\bin\node_modules\@oai\sky\bin\windows\codex-computer-use.exe
```

Original SHA-256:

```text
14d5e9c7336dd34aa8476f218dd45e033b8416bdad6c58fa79c84169ae59f2f3
```

The complete original 42-byte predicate sequence from [heelee912/codex commit 95ee61d](https://github.com/heelee912/codex/commit/95ee61db4a387944889edc9a5b6e97272c8fca9d) occurred exactly once in this 0.7.8 file, at the same file offset, `0x1B6C6`.

The published script was **not** run with its hash guard disabled. Instead, this installation's original whole-file hash, the exact original instruction sequence, its uniqueness, and its offset were checked before a local adaptation.

The correction replaces the localized-role string predicate with:

```text
successful CachedControlType read
AND CachedControlType == UIA_DocumentControlTypeId (50030)
```

A failed getter or a non-document type follows the non-candidate path. The later RootWebArea/value checks and all bytes outside the 42-byte region were left unchanged. This does not inject a URL, force a successful policy result, or disable URL/permission enforcement.

Validation of the file modification:
- Original file backed up and backup SHA-256 verified.
- 42-byte region replaced; 36 bytes actually differ.
- Complete modified file read back and compared with the expected image.
- No changes outside that region.

Modified SHA-256:

```text
08a7a2a9b94ef1c63b935d0424c04289fffbef8c766cab7b7cde67ab68c0f277
```

As expected, modifying the signed executable makes Authenticode report `HashMismatch`. This is an unsupported local workaround, not an official signed fix. No binaries are attached or distributed.

## Actual native Computer Use results afterward

Validation used `@oai/sky` native APIs, not extension-backed Browser Use as a substitute.

| Check | Chrome | Edge |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Native accessibility tree and screenshot returned | Passed | Passed |
| Navigate through the native address-bar control to the public Selenium web form | Passed | Passed |
| Click the Text input control | Passed | Passed after refreshing window/geometry |
| Set test text through native `sky.set_value` | Passed | Passed |
| Read back the exact text in the native tree and screenshot | Passed | Passed |
| Clear test text and restore the original New Tab page | Passed | Passed |

No browser-URL confidence error recurred during these checks. Screenshot-plus-text and text-only state requests succeeded. Screenshot-only requests were not separately tested.

Ordinary minimized-window, user-input-detected, and one click-geometry precondition occurred during validation and were handled by fresh observation/activation. Those checks were not disabled. Some structured `focused_element` results still referred to the address bar after a click, so this report does not claim that every native focus/geometry issue is resolved. Writing was verified through an explicitly targeted native control and actual content readback.

## Scope and limitations

- This is before/after evidence for this particular installation and predicate change, not proof that every report with this error has the same cause.
- We did not instrument the live UIA getter values on this machine, nor perform a full restore/reapply runtime experiment.
- Persistence across a complete desktop restart or a future update has not been tested; updates may replace the local correction.
- A separate browser-tool networking problem was resolved by routing the tool process through the configured proxy. Extension-backed page reading/writing worked before the native correction. Proxy success alone did not repair the native URL failure.

## Requested upstream fix

Please:
1. Classify document controls using successful numeric ControlType reads rather than localized display text.
2. Preserve the existing URL parsing, window identity, candidate validation, and access-policy enforcement.
3. Cover zh-CN/ko-KR and other localized document names, non-document controls named "document", and getter failures in regression tests.
4. Link the official source-level fix and the first signed desktop/runtime release containing it.

Only public test-page details and component metadata are included; no private page contents, account details, screenshots, user-specific paths, or raw logs are attached.

items.body:
## Summary
I am encountering two disruptive problems in the local-task workflow. I do not know whether they share a root cause:

1. A completed local task cannot be opened normally in the chat UI: the conversation stays blank with a central spinner and the composer displays **“Loading model…”**.
2. On the previous day, explicitly authorized work repeatedly failed when instructions were forwarded from the main assistant conversation to local tasks. Repeated confirmation and replacement-task attempts did not reliably resolve this.

## Environment
- Linux web client with a connected, authorized Fedora workstation executing local tasks.
- Exact app/build, browser version, model and Fedora version have not been captured for this report.
- Observed on 15–16 October 2026. Times below are UTC.
- This is a local-task/chat integration report, not a confirmed CLI defect. Please redirect if this belongs in a different tracker.

## Chat loading failure: observed sequence
1. On 16 October around 06:09, a new local task successfully ran a read-only command.
2. Around 06:11, a subsequent coding task completed and reported passing focused checks.
3. Around 06:32, I tried to use that task's chat and could not: the page showed a blank conversation, central loading spinner and “Loading model…” in the composer.
4. Around 06:33, the main assistant successfully sent a diagnostic continuation to the same task. That task ran `pwd` successfully and completed, while the user-facing loading problem remained unresolved.
5. The workstation was still reported connected and authorized during these checks.

This suggests that a successful task admission/execution check is insufficient to establish that the user can open and continue its chat. It does not establish the cause of the loading failure.

## Repeated authorization/task-start failures
During 15 October, the main conversation repeatedly reported that local tasks rejected forwarded requests despite my explicit instructions to perform the work. I was repeatedly asked to reconfirm or use the task directly, undermining remote delegation.

Relevant reported outcomes:
- Around 20:18–20:24: replacement local-task creation initially rejected; a later new task did succeed and complete work.
- Around 20:39–20:40: a subsequent small UI-change instruction was reported rejected when forwarded to the task.
- Around 20:48–20:53: another new-task attempt returned an “outcome unknown” error; a follow-up check found no new task.
- On 16 October around 05:56: the main conversation reported `thread_list_unavailable` despite the workstation being connected and authorized.
- Later on 16 October, task creation and continuation succeeded, but the user-facing chat still failed to load.

These earlier error descriptions are taken from the assistant's contemporaneous reports, not independently captured raw authorization-service logs. Please investigate how explicit user authorization and task lifecycle state are carried between the main conversation and local tasks.

## Expected behavior
- Explicitly authorized, bounded work should be handed to the intended local task without repeated redundant confirmations or inconsistent authorization rejection.
- Task creation failures should have a clear, reconcilable outcome.
- A task that can execute and accept continuation should load its conversation and composer for the user, or display an actionable error instead of an indefinite spinner.

## Impact / current status
This has repeatedly blocked both remote delegation and direct interaction with task chats, requiring retries and prompting consideration of returning to the CLI. A full system update and reboot is planned, but its outcome is not yet known. Reloading the page was suggested; no verified result is available.

## Summary

Browser control in ChatGPT Work, started from the Chrome side panel, fails during initialization before any tab can be read or controlled.

Two supported Browser bootstrap attempts and one page-independent diagnostic attempt in the same conversation all returned the same error after approximately one minute. The failure was observable without a particular website or DOM operation.

This appears closely related to #54376, especially https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/54376#issuecomment-6204588964, and #54484. This report adds observations from an affected macOS session; it does not establish a shared root cause.

## Environment

- Client: ChatGPT/Codex desktop app on macOS, Apple Silicon (arm64).
- Later desktop client metadata in the same conversation reports version `26.1007.71326`. The About dialog was not independently inspected, and the desktop version was not captured at the time of the initial side-panel failure.
- Affected workflow: ChatGPT Work in the Google Chrome extension side panel.
- Exact macOS version, full Chrome version, and installed extension version: not independently captured.
- The assistant's shell environment is a separate Linux environment. No Mac filesystem, native-host configuration, Chrome logs, or desktop-app logs were inspected during these tests.

## Steps to reproduce

Observed in the affected session on October 16, 2026 (Asia/Tokyo):

1. Open a Work conversation from the ChatGPT Chrome extension side panel.
2. Ask the assistant to inspect or control the connected Chrome browser.
3. Invoke the supported Browser JavaScript tool with the documented bootstrap:

```js
const agent = await setupBrowserRuntime();
const browser = await agent.browsers.get("extension");
await nodeRepl.write(await browser.documentation());
```

4. The tool remains pending for approximately one minute and then returns the error below. No browser documentation or page state is returned.

A separate, page-independent diagnostic attempt also returned the same error:

```js
await nodeRepl.write({ diagnostic: "execution_check" });
```

That attempt was intended to check whether a minimal response could be returned without inspecting or modifying a page. Its failure does not establish that the JavaScript body was actually executed.

## Actual result

```text
McpServerError: Sheep MCP session closed: RPC INTERNAL
```

Structured error details returned by the tool:

```json
{
  "error_code": "UNAVAILABLE",
  "error_data": {
    "type": "json_rpc_error",
    "code": -32000,
    "message": "Sheep MCP session closed: RPC INTERNAL"
  }
}
```

Observed attempts:

| Attempt | Operation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Supported Browser bootstrap | Pending for about one minute, then the error above |
| 2 | Page-independent diagnostic response | Pending for about one minute, then the same error |
| 3 | Later retry of the supported bootstrap, around 14:44 JST | Pending for about one minute, then the same error |

The first two tests took place in the conversation started around 14:22 JST. Durations are approximate observations, not a precisely instrumented benchmark.

The user reports that browser control had previously worked. An earlier successful run was not independently captured by this diagnostic.

## Separate later observation

Around 14:51 JST, the same conversation no longer exposed the Browser JavaScript tool, so further connection tests could not be issued. I have not established whether that was caused by the RPC failure, a change in chat surface or plugin attachment, or something else. It should not be treated as proof of an account entitlement change.

The supported Browser tool should initialize and return browser documentation or state, then allow authorized Chrome-tab operations. If initialization fails, it should identify the failing connection stage and provide an actionable recovery message.

The tests establish a repeated initialization failure before page interaction. They do not identify whether the problem is in the extension runtime, session routing, account configuration, or the browser-connection service.

Please investigate the affected side-panel Work initialization path and advise on a supported recovery procedure. If this shares the same cause as #54376, please consolidate this reproduction there.

## Background

As a long-term Codex user, I sometimes develop a strong preference for one particular conversation after spending significant time interacting with it.

Even when conversations use the same underlying model, each has its own history, context, and established communication patterns. I want to preserve and continue the original conversation itself—not export its history and start a different assistant that imitates it.

## Requested feature

Please allow a user to designate an **existing Codex conversation** as a **persistent primary session** that authorized interfaces can access.

1. **Original conversation continuity:** Keep the original conversation/thread identity, history, and available state.
2. **Cross-device access:** Resume the same session from computers, phones, tablets, and other authorized devices.
3. **Third-party integration:** Offer a secure, supported interface for personal web apps, custom chat frontends, and messaging services to access *that specific existing conversation*.
4. **Shared history:** Route messages sent through those authorized interfaces into the same thread, rather than creating separate conversations.
5. **Subscription-based usage:** Where subscription terms and product design permit, count such interactions toward the user's existing ChatGPT/Codex allowance.
6. **Local-hosted first:** It would be useful even if the computer hosting the session must remain online; cloud-hosted continuity could come later.
7. **Permission controls:** Require explicit authorization, scoped access, device management, and revocation.

## Why it matters

Some people use Codex not only for coding or short tasks, but also as a long-term working partner and conversational companion. After weeks or months, familiarity and accumulated context can make one specific conversation especially valuable. Starting a new session with copied memories does not provide the same continuity.

**The goal is not to create another AI assistant. The goal is to keep talking with the exact existing Codex conversation the user has chosen, across their authorized devices and apps.**

Thank you for considering this feature.

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?
ChatGPT desktop 26.1013.31256, build 20586, production channel. The macOS bundle identifier is `com.openai.codex`. The integrated update check reports `up_to_date`.

### What subscription do you have?
Not collected in the diagnostic report; this is a signed-in personal account. I can provide account-specific details privately if needed.

### What platform is your computer?
macOS 27.0.1 (26A434), Apple Silicon / arm64.
Microsoft Edge 155.0.4283.45.
Official ChatGPT extension from the Chrome Web Store, installed **inside Edge**: `hehggadaopoacecdllhhajmbjkdcmajg`, version 1.26.1005.11759.

### What issue are you seeing?
In the native desktop app's **normal Chat mode**, `Browser.list_tabs` is exposed but fails with:

```text
UNKNOWN: Error code: UNKNOWN; Error:
RuntimeException: Browser access requires the originating browser context.
Open ChatGPT in the browser with the connected extension and try again.
```

The same failure is reported in both the existing Chat and a **new normal Chat created directly in the desktop app**. Work succeeds in the same desktop app and is used below only as a comparison.

The extension/local bridge is healthy: the bundled extension-installation and native-host-manifest diagnostics both pass. Work in the same desktop app can discover Edge, list tabs, read a public page, follow its link, go back, reload, and read again.

| Surface / check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Normal Chat on ChatGPT Web in Edge | User previously confirmed successful tab listing |
| Bundled extension check | Installed and enabled |
| Bundled native-host manifest check | `correct=true`, no missing origins |
| Desktop Work: Edge discovery and tab listing | Pass |
| Desktop Work: public page read, navigation, back, reload | Pass |
| Existing normal desktop Chat: `Browser.list_tabs` | Fails with the error above |
| New normal desktop Chat: `Browser.list_tabs` | Same failure |
| Chat page reading | Not attempted after enumeration failed |

### What steps can reproduce the bug?
1. Install/enable the official ChatGPT Chrome Web Store extension in Microsoft Edge, and keep the desktop app running.
2. Confirm that both official bundled diagnostics pass:
   - `check-extension-installed.js --browser edge --json`
   - `check-native-host-manifest.js --browser edge --json`
3. Verify Edge access from desktop Work using only a public page. In this case, tab listing, reading `example.com`, following its IANA link, going back, and reloading all succeeded.
4. Create a new **normal Chat directly in the desktop app**, rather than on the web or in the extension sidebar.
5. Request an actual `Browser.list_tabs` call. In the test below it returned the originating-browser-context error, without returning a tab list.

**Test-method limitation:** the user created the new Chat directly in the desktop UI, then a local diagnostic Work task opened it with `navigate_to_codex_page` and submitted the test with `send_message_to_thread`. The Chat's response reports the real Browser call and exact error; `read_thread` exposes that request/response but not the raw internal Browser trace. A directly hand-typed desktop-composer A/B test was not independently captured. Please consider whether the cross-chat submission path is relevant. The receiving Chat also reported that it did not have sufficient metadata to independently identify its surface.

No web-search/fetch fallback was counted as browser success. No private tab contents were read. Private conversation IDs and account identifiers are omitted from this public issue.

### What is the expected behavior?
Normal desktop Chat should receive the authorized originating browser context when Browser tools are available, or clearly explain that the operation is unsupported on that surface. A healthy extension and native bridge should not lead to a tool being exposed that can only return a missing-origin-context exception.

### Additional information
#### Read-only inspection of the installed desktop bundle
The installed `webview/index.html` loads an entry point referencing:

```text
webview/assets/app-initial-3ccf4886957f.js
SHA-256: d6278b4127345cf6012fe969eea9f5a2d55a13225d1fcadc23db81ef5bab78fe
```

The following minified identifiers are specific to this build. Relevant excerpts:

```js
function ROt(){return VOt}
function zOt(e){VOt?.setLocation(e)}
function BOt(e){return VOt!=null&&(VOt.setAuthState(e),!0)}
var VOt;
function HOt(){return(HOt=t((()=>{})))()}
```

Within this module, the bridge variable `VOt` is declared but no assignment to it was found. Context preparation exits if that bridge is absent:

```js
function jqa(e){let t=ROt();if(t==null)return; /* ... t.prepareSubmit(...) ... */ }
```

The shared Chat submission pipeline calls `jqa(e)` and passes its optional `w?.context` as `sideChatContext` to the request builder. The only `browser_context` assignment found in this module is guarded by that context:

```js
function Mqa(e,t,n){
  if(t==null)return;
  e.client_contextual_info={app_name:`chatgpt.com`,app_surface:`browser_side_chat`};
  e.browser_context={instance_id:t.instanceId};
  // ...
}
```

The Chat fallback used by `send_message_to_thread` (`Gfo` → `Rfo`) reaches the shared `Hro` submission pipeline. Another UI submission call site also reaches `Hro`.

**Hypothesis, not a verified server root cause:** this native build appears to leave the side-chat context bridge uninitialized, causing `browser_context.instance_id` to be omitted. That is consistent with the returned exception. We did not capture the native outbound request or inspect the backend guard, so this does not establish every possible injection/routing path or prove that the cross-chat test is identical to a manually typed desktop request.

#### Follow-up: request construction, serialization, and available runtime evidence

**The native outbound HTTP request has not been captured.** The following findings combine read-only inspection of the distributed client with existing desktop logs; they are not a network trace or proof of the body received by the backend.

- The request preparation path described above passes the optional context from `jqa()` through `Hro()` to `UJa()` / `Mqa()`. In the inspected desktop module, no initialization assignment to the bridge variable `VOt` was found. With no bridge/context, `Mqa()` returns before adding `browser_context.instance_id`.
- Following the code further, `hqr()` constructs the POST to `/f/conversation` using `JSON.stringify(e)`. Its pre-dispatch path updates `client_prepare_state` and may add `app_attest_challenge`; the inspected branches do not add browser context.
- A scan of all distributed JavaScript modules under `/webview` and `/.vite` found one assignment that adds `browser_context` to a Chat request body: the `Mqa()` assignment shown above. The other two textual occurrences are cloud-browser-context deletion endpoints in settings, not desktop Chat context initialization.
- We examined 37 desktop log files for October 16, 2026 (approximately 4.4 MB). They do not expose Chat HTTP request bodies. Text matches inside diagnostic-task reasoning summaries were excluded as evidence of network traffic.
- The active session's startup log at `2026-10-16T05:54:16.684Z` reports `allowDebugMenu=false allowDevtools=false allowInspectElement=false buildFlavor=prod packaged=true`. This confirms the production inspection settings, not the contents of an outbound request.

**Interpretation:** the evidence points to context being omitted during client request construction, before serialization, rather than demonstrating that context is lost in transport. This remains an inference about the live request. We have not observed the actual native request body, the backend's context association, or the server-side guard that raises the exception. The cross-chat submission limitation documented above still applies.

A fix in the official client could supply the authorized browser context to the request builder. These findings do **not** establish that a server-side change is mandatory, nor that a local preference can repair the native tool. No supported local setting that initializes this context was identified.

To resolve the remaining uncertainty, a supported native-request capture or an OpenAI-side trace would need to establish whether `browser_context` / `instance_id` are present, alongside the request ID, timestamp, and client surface. Private prompts, cookies, and tokens are not needed in a public report.

items.body:
# Windows: repeated WSL workspace probes and WSLg trace-log accumulation associated with disk exhaustion and system instability

### Summary and impact

**Impact: maximum disk-space usage (effective disk exhaustion) and system instability, as reported by the owner.** The initial system-drive measurement showed only **1,388,544 bytes (approximately 1.32 MiB) free**. Diagnostic traces accounted for **40.55 GiB** of storage. That is the measured trace-folder size, not a configured cap or a verified all-time maximum.

A WSL-hosted project remained attached to Codex Desktop on Windows after its command runner had failed to start. Later, Procmon recorded repeated repository/configuration probes of that project's `\\wsl.localhost` path by the **Codex Desktop app-server**. Nearby WSLg Remote Desktop connection cycles generated diagnostic traces on the Windows system drive.

The incident involved accumulating trace logs, loss of usable disk capacity, and reported system instability; a memory leak has not been demonstrated. Other storage consumers were present, so the measurements do not attribute every consumed byte or each instability symptom solely to these logs. Insufficient Git permissions were initially suspected, but the capture does not establish a Git permission failure or an exclusive causal chain from Codex to all historical log growth.

**Why this is easy to miss:** disk consumption increases gradually alongside normal Codex use, making it easy to confuse with storage growth from new chats, expanding workspaces/worktrees, dependency caches, and other routine Codex work. Users may attribute the shrinking free space to expected project activity, delaying recognition of the accumulating diagnostic traces until disk capacity and system stability are affected. New chats and workspace expansion are potential sources of misattribution here, not established triggers of the trace growth.

**Current status: resolved on the affected machine after a combination of actions reported by the owner:**

- Archival/removal of the project from Codex Desktop.
- Restarting Codex CLI on both Windows and WSL.
- Deleting the project folder on WSL.

These actions were combined, so the necessary or sufficient action has not been isolated. This records the owner's successful recovery, not a verified upstream software fix. Folder deletion is part of the incident history, not a proposed general fix for other users.

### Environment

| Component | Observed value |
|---|---|
| Codex Desktop | Installed package `OpenAI.Codex_26.1007.9446.0_x64`; About-dialog version not separately collected |
| Windows | x64, version `10.0.26200.9711`, display version `25H2` |
| WSL | `2.6.3.0` |
| Linux kernel | `6.6.87.2-1` |
| WSL distribution | `Ubuntu-24.04` |
| WSLg | `1.0.71` |
| WSL Remote Desktop client | `msrdc.exe` file version `1.2.6353.0` |
| Procmon | Microsoft-signed `4.12` |
| CLI versions / subscription | Not collected |

The affected path, with private details replaced, was:

```text
\\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu-24.04\home\<linux-user>\<projects>\<project>
```

Before the owner's folder deletion, the WSL project directory existed but its `.git` entry did not. A separate Windows checkout had a `.git` entry. No evidence establishes how the WSL directory originally lost or lacked its Git metadata. The earlier chat reported an attached workspace whose command runner could not start; it did not identify the underlying failure.

### Captured behavior

Procmon used one include rule, `Path contains wsl.localhost`, with Drop Filtered Events enabled and a bounded 180-second runtime. Collection ran from **2026-10-16 02:59:45.602 to 03:02:52.924 UTC**, including startup/shutdown.

- All **890** exported events matched the filter. **838 (94.2%)** came from `codex.exe`, PID 30552, in `app-server` mode.
- Both live process metadata and the trace identified its parent as `ChatGPT.exe` within the installed Codex Desktop package. The captured caller was therefore the desktop backend; the `codex.exe` filename alone would not distinguish it from CLI.
- Requests repeatedly probed `.git`, `.codex`, and ancestor directories. Results included **248 NAME NOT FOUND**, **26 PATH NOT FOUND**, and **480 SUCCESS** events. The remaining results were NOT SUPPORTED, FAST IO DISALLOWED, and BUFFER OVERFLOW. **No ACCESS DENIED result occurred among those 838 events.**
- One direct Codex probe burst began at **03:02:08.203 UTC**, followed by an RDP connection attempt at **03:02:08.619** and a successful connection at **03:02:09.036**. The initial gap was **0.417 seconds**. Probe bursts were not uniformly once per minute.
- WSL's `msrdc.exe` referenced `wslg.rdp`. The RDP operational log repeatedly showed event IDs 1024/1025/1033/1105/1026, including `SL::OnDisconnected` with error `0x904`.

Traces accumulated under:

```text
%LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp\DiagOutputDir\RdClientAutoTrace
```

The folder initially contained **43,543,703,552 bytes (40.55 GiB)**. Removing **2,109 files older than 24 hours** reclaimed **42,578,477,056 bytes (39.654 GiB)**, retaining recent traces. That cleanup alone did not stop accumulation: approximately **9 hours 25 minutes later**, the folder was back to roughly **10 GB** total (measured **9.15 GB / 8.525 GiB**).

| Event on October 15, 2026 | Local time (EDT) | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Old-log deletion | Approximately 1:19–1:21 PM | Command launched at 1:19:09 PM; successful completion reported at 1:20:51 PM; 52 recent trace/event-processor files retained |
| Subsequent size measurement | 10:45:36 PM | 204 files totaling 9,153,548,288 bytes (9.15 GB / 8.525 GiB) |
| Approximate interval | 9 hours 25–26 minutes | About 9.5 hours from the deletion window to the later measurement |

The later total is rounded to roughly 10 GB for impact reporting. The exact time the folder crossed 10 GB was not observed, and the retained recent logs mean this is not a measurement of 10 GB of entirely new writes.

### Reproduction status

A minimal, deterministic reproducer has **not** been established. The observed setup was a retained WSL UNC workspace with prior command-runner failure and missing Git metadata, followed by repeated backend filesystem probes and nearby WSLg connection cycles.

For investigation, a disposable WSL workspace could be used to compare valid Git metadata, missing metadata, and denied access independently, then compare project removal and process restarts separately. These are proposed isolation tests, not tests already completed. Ordinary project folders without Git should remain supported.

### Expected behavior

- Workspace access failures should produce an actionable error and bounded retries/backoff, without repeatedly waking WSL when the project is inactive.
- Removing a project should release associated background monitoring and repository discovery across relevant processes.
- A missing `.git` directory should be handled as a non-repository condition without an indefinite retry cycle.
- The interaction with WSLg should not result in persistent connection churn and trace-log accumulation that exhausts available disk space and destabilizes the system. The trace producer and retention behavior may require separate Microsoft investigation.

### Recovery evidence and limits

A second capture used the same filter and a 90-second runtime, spanning **2026-10-16 03:20:04.095–03:21:42.769 UTC**, including startup/shutdown. It contained **zero matching share accesses**. The enabled RDP operational log contained **zero events 1024/1025/1026/1033** in that interval.

The exact timing of each owner action relative to this capture was not recorded. The owner subsequently confirmed resolution after the combined Desktop project removal/archival, Windows and WSL CLI restarts, and WSL folder deletion. The quiet capture supports absence of the earlier pattern during that interval; it is not a long-term ETL growth measurement.

There were other WSL activators during the first capture: the investigation's own local reporting hooks invoked WSL, and Docker performed a separate WSL lifecycle operation. These confounders prevent assigning every reconnect or the entire historical trace volume to Codex workspace probing. The ETL files were produced by Microsoft's WSLg Remote Desktop client, not by Codex's conversation storage.

Raw PML/XML files remain local because they contain private paths and process command lines. Only sanitized counts, timing, ancestry, and error summaries are included here.

### Related reports

- [openai/codex #41147](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/41147): internal Git snapshots hash large untracked files into `.git/objects`, filling the WSL virtual disk. This shares the disk-exhaustion impact, but the storage growth measured here was Windows-side `RdClientAutoTrace` ETL data written by WSLg's `msrdc.exe`; this investigation did not establish Git snapshot/object growth as its cause.
- [openai/codex #38079](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/38079): increasing `wslservice.exe` handles/threads and lingering `node_repl.exe` processes during native Windows tool calls, with service-resource recovery requiring a WSL service restart. This shares gradual degradation and system instability, but it does not document the ETL accumulation measured here. This investigation did not measure a handle/thread leak.
- [openai/codex #30048](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/30048): unwanted WSL startup from Codex Desktop. Related activation behavior; does not establish this log-growth failure.
- [openai/codex #46640](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/46640): Windows sandbox ACL initialization failures for WSL UNC workspaces. A possible related failure class, not evidence that this incident had the same cause.
- [microsoft/WSL #41418](https://github.com/microsoft/WSL/issues/41418): repeated WSLg Remote Desktop connection cycles, `0x904`, and ETL accumulation; a contributor identified periodic WSL share access as a VM wakeup trigger.

**Duplicate assessment:** related, but not established duplicates of #41147 or #38079. The measured resource, storage location, and immediate producer differ. A shared upstream cause remains possible; these observations support keeping the trace-log failure separately identifiable and cross-linking the reports pending maintainer investigation.

Targeted searches for `RdClientAutoTrace`, `WSL msrdc`, and `wsl.localhost`, followed by direct review of #41147 and #38079 and their available comments, found no confirmed exact match for this captured workspace-probing/log-growth combination. This was not an exhaustive duplicate search.

Title: iOS Remote: new chats appear to lose secondary folders from multi-folder desktop projects

Summary
A local desktop project has a custom display name and two attached Git repositories. In Codex on iOS, connected to the same Mac, the project is listed under the primary folder's basename. More importantly, when starting a new chat from that mobile project entry, the user reports that the agent only recognizes the primary repository rather than both attached repositories.

Environment
- Host: macOS 26.5.2.
- Desktop app: ChatGPT / Codex, bundle identifier com.openai.codex, version 26.1007.71326, build 20398.
- Client: ChatGPT on iPhone, Codex connected to the Mac host.
- iOS version and mobile app version: not collected.
- First observed: October 15, 2026, America/Vancouver.

Steps to reproduce
1. On desktop, create a local project with a custom name such as "Example Project".
2. Attach two separate Git repository folders, for example "docs-repo" as primary and "app-repo" as secondary.
3. Start a desktop chat and confirm both folders are included in the workspace.
4. Connect ChatGPT on iPhone to that same Mac host and open Codex.
5. Find the project; it appears under "docs-repo" rather than "Example Project".
6. Start a new chat from that mobile project entry.
7. Ask the agent to identify its attached workspace roots and work across both repositories. Compare the result with the desktop-created chat.

Expected behavior
The mobile-created chat should preserve the saved desktop project's identity and attached folder set, including both repositories. If starting a multi-folder project from mobile is unsupported, the UI should explain that limitation before starting a chat with reduced context.

Actual behavior
- Screenshot evidence: mobile displays the primary folder basename instead of the saved project name; the Mac host is shown connected.
- User observation: new mobile-created chats recognize only the primary repository.
- Verified desktop evidence: the saved local project configuration contains both folders in its rootPaths array, and the desktop-origin chat's current workspace roots include both repositories.

Evidence limits / investigation request
The missing secondary-folder behavior was reported by the user; this investigation did not independently inspect a newly created failing mobile chat's workspace roots or reproduce a permission-denied operation. Please check whether mobile chat creation resolves the project by its primary path and fails to carry the saved project ID and additional roots, versus merely failing to surface the secondary folder to the agent. This is a hypothesis, not an established root cause.

Impact
A project that combines product/documentation context and implementation repositories appears to lose part of its workspace when started from mobile. The user cannot confidently rely on mobile-created chats having the same context as desktop-created chats.

Related issue
https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/36754 documents a similar primary-basename versus saved-name mismatch on Windows/Android. This report adds an iOS/macOS observation and a separate apparent loss of secondary-folder context.

References
https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/projects?surface=app describes local projects with multiple attached folders and secondary-folder access.
https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/remote-connections describes remote access using the connected host's projects and files.

Privacy
Project and folder names above are generic placeholders. No private repository contents, absolute paths, hostnames, account identifiers, project IDs, screenshots, session transcripts, or logs are attached.

### Summary
A Plus subscriber who had connected a separate Gmail address for Gmail data access found that **Codex Desktop was signed in as the Gmail-address identity (Free)** rather than the subscriber's original ChatGPT Plus account. The user believed the Gmail integration was attached to their existing Plus account, not that the Gmail address could be selected as a *different ChatGPT sign-in identity*.

Consequences:
- Codex Desktop showed **Free** and prompted to upgrade, while ChatGPT Web and Codex Web showed normal Plus entitlements.
- The expected personalized avatar/profile did not appear.
- The user's previously visible **banked usage resets** appeared to be missing (they were not actually lost).
- Repeatedly signing out/in on desktop did not help, because the browser's "Welcome back / choose an account" screen kept offering the remembered Gmail-address account.
- Another PC using the original account showed the expected Plus subscription.

### User Impact

This is more than an authentication issue. It is a user experience issue.

I am a long-term ChatGPT Plus subscriber with some technical and software development experience. Yet it still took considerable time and multiple troubleshooting attempts to identify what turned out to be a simple account-selection problem.


Users should not need to understand OAuth, account identities, or subscription mechanisms just to access a product they already pay for.

I hope OpenAI will pay as much attention to making AI accessible and frustration-free as it does to improving model intelligence.

### Observed resolution
On the Codex browser-based sign-in page, a remembered account tile showed the Gmail-address identity. Below it there was a **"Use another account"** option. Choosing that and explicitly signing in with the original ChatGPT Plus account immediately restored **Plus**, the correct avatar, and the banked resets.

### Expected UX
- Make the distinction between **connecting a Gmail inbox as a data source** and **signing in to ChatGPT/Codex with a Google/Gmail identity** much clearer.
- Clearly indicate the email and entitlement (Free versus Plus) of the account that Codex is about to authenticate, and allow easy account switching.
- Provide a prominent "Wrong account? Use a different ChatGPT account" action if desktop claims Free while the user's expected entitlements are on another account.
- Avoid creating the impression that previously held purchased or banked resources vanished because of a remembered account selection.

### Notes / limits
- This is a **confirmed account-selection/UX failure mode**, **not evidence** that linking the Gmail connector changes the primary account email or automatically creates a new OpenAI account. The exact moment when the Gmail identity first acquired a separate OpenAI sign-in session is unknown.

Add `write_file_stream` to `ExecutorFileSystem` and `EnvironmentAccess`, preserving the accessor's captured sandbox permissions. Close remote handles on completion or failure, perform best-effort cleanup after cancellation, and invalidate pending metadata lookups. Document that failure or cancellation can leave a truncated or partial file and that in-flight I/O may outlive cancellation.

Add coverage for sequential writes, binary and empty files across local and remote filesystems, source failures, handle cleanup, metadata invalidation after cancellation, and compatibility with older executors.

The sidebar shows a section named `Life`, with entries such as `Work_Garden`, `了解 Zotero 组织结构与 AI 协作`, and `审计项目工作链路漏洞` displayed as independent chat rows, without the expected project folder grouping/icon. The user confirms that they explicitly created the Life project rather than merely starting a general chat. The new project is not represented in the same way as older projects.

Creating/adding a local project should register and display that project as a folder/group in the sidebar, and its chats should be organized under it, consistent with existing local projects.

## Steps to reproduce (user-reported; not independently verified)
1. Open Codex Desktop on Windows, version 26.1007.71326.
2. Create/add a new project (e.g. `Life`).
3. Start conversations associated with it.
4. Observe that they appear as standalone conversation entries rather than under a folder-icon project entry.
5. Compare with existing projects, which remain represented as project folders.

## Impact
New projects are not clearly grouped or navigable like previously created projects, disrupting the project-based workflow. No file or conversation data loss has been confirmed.

## Related reports
- #53251 — Windows Codex Desktop sidebar loses local projects after update/restart (version 26.1007 series).
- #39489 — New Chat from Local Project creates a global chat instead of a project chat (macOS).
- #46987 — Project/thread grouping lost after desktop state corruption.

items.body:
## Summary

In the Windows Codex desktop app, long-running coding sessions that previously inspected images continue producing very large model request bodies after new image inspection has stopped. Client compression logs and a read-only local proxy traffic sample corroborate repeated tens-of-megabytes upstream requests. Connection failures/retries amplify the bandwidth cost.

Please investigate image/context reuse, incremental transport, and bandwidth-aware retry behavior. This report separates observed measurements from the suspected root cause; no payload decryption or fresh reproduction was performed.

## Environment

- Windows 11 Pro, 10.0.26200, x64
- Installed desktop package: OpenAI.Codex 26.1007.9446.0
- Bundled executable reports: codex-cli 0.162.0-alpha.17.2
- Model reported in client logs: gpt-6.1-sol
- Existing long-running local coding workflow with multiple agent contexts and earlier local-image inspection
- HTTP Responses transport; local Proxifier → v2rayN/sing-box proxy chain. Network failures are present, so the proxy/network is a confounding factor for retry frequency.
- Observation date: 2026-10-16, times below UTC+08:00

## Observed client request sizes

Read-only analysis of `codex_http_client::request` entries containing `Compressed request body with zstd`:

| Anonymized context | Observed interval | Encoded request bodies | Median compressed size | Sum of encoded compressed bodies |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| A | 09:56–10:55 | 73 | 43.62 MiB | 2966.7 MiB |
| B | 10:41–11:31 | 70 | 35.37 MiB | 2476.4 MiB |
| Coordinator | 10:56–11:31 | 53 | 6.16 MiB | 327.0 MiB |
| C | 10:43–10:46 | 7 | 15.61 MiB | 100.5 MiB |

The total logged compressed body size in this available sample is 5870.4 MiB. This is **encoded/prepared request volume, not a claim that every byte was successfully transmitted**; some requests failed.

Representative sanitized lines from context B:

```text
11:29:06 pre_compression_bytes=50307725 post_compression_bytes=37235458
11:29:48 pre_compression_bytes=50317761 post_compression_bytes=37241443
11:30:16 pre_compression_bytes=50321159 post_compression_bytes=37243494
11:31:03 pre_compression_bytes=50331169 post_compression_bytes=37250681
11:31:47 pre_compression_bytes=50348346 post_compression_bytes=37260222
```

Transport/client logs identify POST `https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses`.

## Independent network corroboration

A ~20.07-second read-only sample of the existing local proxy connection counters measured:

- Total upstream delta: 37,388,714 bytes
- One `chatgpt.com` TCP connection accounted for 37,312,985 upstream bytes and only 2,981 downstream bytes during that interval
- That connection began at 11:29:48, closely matching the timestamp and compressed size of the model request logged above

This corroborates actual large transfers rather than merely large local log files. The user reports sustained upstream traffic around 1–2 MB/s over hours; the sample is consistent with repeated large requests, but is not itself a full multi-hour packet trace.

## Evidence pointing to retained image context

Context B's session log contains 11 image entries totaling 48,680,818 bytes of image data-URL text. Its last new image entry is timestamped 10:19:45. Later requests from 10:41 through 11:31 still have ~50.3 MB pre-compression / ~37.3 MB post-compression bodies.

Context A's image data-URL text totals 63,337,916 bytes; later request bodies reach ~65.5 MB before compression / ~48.8 MB afterward.

The size correspondence and the absence of new images for over an hour in B strongly suggest retained images are repeatedly carried in subsequent model context. **We have not decrypted or compared actual request bodies byte-for-byte, so the precise serialization/cache mechanism remains a hypothesis, not a confirmed source-level defect.**

## Retries / failures

- Context B has 46 logged POST `/codex/responses` send-failure entries in the observed interval.
- Logs include `stream connection failed; waiting to retry ... retry_delay=5s` and retry exhaustion / timeout messages.
- Failed attempts may have transmitted only part of a request; the encoded-byte totals must not be treated as exact billed/network totals.

## Expected behavior / requested improvements

1. Reuse already-uploaded image content via an appropriate reference/session mechanism where possible; avoid resending full historical image data for each text/code sampling step.
2. Prevent full image-history duplication when handing off to another agent/context, or make that cost visible and controllable.
3. Expose outbound request size / accumulated upload volume so users can identify a large-context bandwidth loop.
4. Make retries bandwidth-aware, with backoff/circuit-breaking and a clear way to halt repeated multi-megabyte uploads.
5. Provide a supported way to retain textual findings while dropping old image payloads from subsequent context.

No images, raw transcripts, project code, credentials, account identifiers, local usernames, private IP addresses, or proxy configuration are attached. This summary was generated from existing local logs and counters without interrupting the running coding task.

## Follow-up observation

The abnormal transfer persisted after diagnosis without a fresh image inspection in this side conversation. A second read-only sample at ~12:25 measured 12,440,409 upstream bytes in 5.03 seconds (~2.47 MB/s); 12,273,988 bytes belonged to one `chatgpt.com` connection. Context B still logged large bodies at 12:24:20, 12:24:52, and 12:25:31, with the latest `pre_compression_bytes=51632195 post_compression_bytes=38104670`. This supports investigating the retained context and ongoing retry/sampling path rather than only the frequency of new image-tool calls. The running main task was not paused or modified by this diagnostic side conversation.

## Observed workflow (not a minimal deterministic reproducer)

1. Use the Windows desktop app for a long-running local coding task, including agent work and earlier local-image inspection.
2. Continue code/text work after the last image inspection.
3. Inspect existing `codex_http_client::request` compression telemetry and independently sample existing proxy byte counters.
4. Observe recurring tens-of-megabytes model requests and substantial upstream traffic; some connections fail and are retried.

## Related reports

- #49738: Windows app upload saturation and network latency.
- #29854: Windows app-server uplink saturation.
- #51889: image/media-heavy history, transport failures, and large HTTP fallback bodies on macOS.

This report adds Windows client compression-byte measurements, a matching live connection-counter sample, and continued large requests long after the last new image entry. It does not claim the exact same underlying cause as those reports.

Submitted by an assistant at the user's explicit request, using sanitized measured diagnostics; no raw files or private session identifiers are included.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Current configured updater result on 2026-10-16: app 26.1013.31256, build 20586, production channel, status `up_to_date`. The installed Windows package is 26.1013.3656.0.

The captured failures occurred with Windows package 26.1007.9446.0. The corresponding About-dialog version at failure time was not recorded. No claim is made that the newer version has or has not fixed this issue; no destructive stress reproduction was attempted.

### What subscription do you have?

Not included in this sanitized report; this is a local background-process/resource-exhaustion incident.

### What platform is your computer?

Windows 11 x64, OS version 10.0.26340, 32 GiB physical RAM.

### What issue are you seeing?

Repeated uncontrolled Git process fan-out under a verified Codex backend exhausts Windows system commit and coincides with desktop hangs/app closures. Two complete process-counter captures on 2026-10-15 recorded:

| Capture (UTC+7) | Simultaneous Git processes | Combined Git private committed bytes | System commit used |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| approximately 20:08 | 5,276 | 92.134 GiB | 99.998% |
| approximately 20:48 | 5,737 | 98.275 GiB | 100% |

All captured Git processes in those peak inventories had valid Codex backend ancestry. Local app metadata contained `watch-repo` and `subscribe-live-query` status activity. These are observed associations; the exact internal scheduling/event loop is not yet identified.

On 2026-10-16 at approximately 08:45 (UTC+7), a local observer counted another 5,378 Codex-descended Git processes. Their subcommands were not retained. Windows recorded system commit exhaustion at 08:45, 08:51 and 09:53, a desktop `ChatGPT.exe` crash at 08:45:55 (exception `e0000008`), and a `codex.exe` failure at 08:46:34 (exception `c0000409`), with packaged Codex WER crash records. A later `ChatGPT.exe` hang was recorded at 10:28:28; its precise cause is unconfirmed because process recording had an earlier gap. Exception codes alone are not treated as a root-cause diagnosis.

An external, status-only cancellation workaround did not cover the October 16 Git command forms and failed under memory pressure. Its recorded cancellations were accounted for by controlled tests, not real incident mitigation. It has been removed from automatic execution. A read-only bounded process recorder is running instead. No wrapper or post-spawn kill mechanism is proposed as the product fix.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

There is no deterministic minimal reproducer yet. The observed usage was the Windows desktop app with multiple existing local coding chats and background repository refreshes. The user was not deliberately launching thousands of Git commands. Multiple active chats are context, not a proven trigger.

Please investigate launch accounting and overlapping refresh/probe requests in Windows repository watchers/live queries and backend Git metadata probes. A safe vendor-side regression test could inject 5,000 repository invalidation events and verify bounded actual child creation, including Git for Windows launcher/child variants. The user machine should not be subjected to that stress test.

### What is the expected behavior?

Bound Git work before process creation, globally and per repository. Coalesce redundant refreshes, single-flight/cache repeatable probes, and bound the pending request queue. Preserve ordering/semantics of writes and return current-generation results. Keep interactive work responsive and recover from child allocation/failure as a repository-status error rather than terminating the app or exhausting the whole machine.

A cap on the entire backend or an external wrapper that leaves thousands of waiting processes is insufficient. Please expose active, queued and coalesced request counts so the fix can be verified without reproducing system exhaustion.

### Additional information

Related report: #54439 describes redundant read-only Git probes on Windows. It is relevant context, but its 16–22 launches per turn are different from the thousands of simultaneous processes captured here; a shared root cause has not been established.

Hardware temperature or defective RAM has not been established as the cause of these Git storms. Separate earlier kernel incidents have not been conflated with this report.

This report intentionally excludes usernames, machine identifiers, repository names, filesystem paths, chat/session identifiers, credentials, source code, raw logs and dumps. No raw attachments are included. Local evidence is retained for a separately reviewed, privacy-safe follow-up if needed.
